Bristol.wildlife_intro:
Bristol's wildlife calls come from the Pequabuck River corridor and the wooded parks threaded through the city. Squirrels are a constant in Federal Hill and Forestville, where mature street trees meet older homes. Raccoons den in chimneys across the older neighborhoods, bats roost in pre-war roofs, and woodchucks burrow under sheds and porches in the roomier suburbs. Rockwell Park and Birge Pond hold foxes and coyotes that are sometimes seen at the edges of nearby streets.

The older housing stock drives most of the actual work: stone foundations let mice and chipmunks in at grade, while settled soffits and old gable vents give squirrels and bats their openings higher up. In spring our crew handles raccoon families, through summer we deal with bats and woodchucks, and in fall mice pour into Bristol homes ahead of the cold. We seal as carefully as we remove — an unsealed entry in these older houses simply gets reused by the next animal.

Enfield.wildlife_intro:
Enfield sits between the Connecticut River and farm country, and our crew sees both sides of that in its calls. River neighborhoods in Thompsonville get raccoons, skunks, and muskrats near wet ground, while the farm edges and the Scantic River corridor in Hazardville bring woodchucks, bats in barns, and mice working in from fields each fall. Squirrels are at home in the mature trees of the postwar suburbs, and bats roost in older village homes in both mill sections of town.

Thompsonville's older housing has the layered roofs and brick chimneys that raccoons and bats prefer, and outbuildings on the farm streets give animals a second target if only the house is sealed. Our crew inspects sheds and barns along with the home, removes animals humanely, and closes the entries we find. In spring, denning season dominates; in late summer and fall, we seal river-town and farm-edge homes before rodents and squirrels claim them for the winter.

Hartford.wildlife_intro:
Hartford's wildlife work is city work: Norway rats in the basements and alleys of triple-decker neighborhoods, raccoons in chimneys from Frog Hollow to the North End, squirrels and pigeons in older roof structures, and bats in the attics of West End and Asylum Hill houses. The Connecticut River floodplain, Keney Park, and the remaining open stretches of the Park River give animals cover inside the city, and dense housing gives them food and shelter within a short nightly walk.

In triple-deckers, one unsealed foundation gap can serve several units, so our crew inspects the whole building rather than a single apartment. Flat roofs and parapets hide squirrel and pigeon entries that are invisible from the street. Cold Connecticut winters push mice and rats indoors across the city, spring brings raccoon mothers into chimneys, and summer brings bat colonies to the older housing stock — with exclusions planned around the June to mid-August pause in CT DEEP guidance.

Manchester.wildlife_intro:
Manchester's calls start with its mill history and its river. The Cheney-era housing near the center gives raccoons and bats chimneys and rooflines they have used for generations, while the Hockanum River and Bigelow Brook corridors move skunks, opossums, and muskrats through the neighborhoods. In the newer Buckland Hills subdivisions, squirrels in attics and woodchucks under decks and sheds are the common calls, and homes backing onto Case Mountain's woods see the heaviest all-around pressure in town.

Our crew handles a lot of squirrel work in Manchester's postwar housing, where mature oaks overhang roofs, and a lot of mice in fall, when field and woods-edge homes take in rodents ahead of winter. Spring litters put raccoon families in chimneys and skunk families under porches. We remove the animals, fit chimney caps, seal the soffit and gable entries we find, and screen decks and sheds so the next family on the Hockanum corridor cannot simply move into the space we emptied.

New Britain.wildlife_intro:
New Britain's dense, older housing gives our crew steady urban work: rats in basements and around older commercial blocks, raccoons in chimneys and flat-roof structures, squirrels chewing into triple-decker rooflines, and bats in the high gables of the older houses near Walnut Hill. Stanley Quarter Park, Martha Hart Park, and the Willow Brook corridor keep woods and water inside the city, so skunks, opossums, and woodchucks also appear in the roomier residential streets at the city's edges.

Multi-family buildings are the heart of the challenge here — a squirrel or rat entry at a shared roofline can affect several households, and sealing one unit rarely solves a building-wide problem. Our crew inspects from foundation to ridge, removes the animals, and seals entries across the structure. Winters are busy with mice and rats moving indoors, spring with denning raccoons, and late summer with homeowners who discover a bat colony has been overhead all season.

West Hartford.wildlife_intro:
West Hartford's mature trees are the story behind most of our calls here. Gray squirrels travel the canopy over the Center and Bishops Corner and drop onto roofs with aging soffits, raccoons use big hollow street trees as home base before moving into chimneys, and bats find the gaps in early-1900s rooflines. Moles work the cared-for lawns throughout town, Trout Brook carries skunks and opossums through the Elmwood side, and the reservoir woods on the western border keep wildlife pressure high on nearby streets.

Our crew does a great deal of careful sealing in West Hartford, because colonials and Tudors with dormers, additions, and layered roofs rarely have just one entry. Winter brings mice into stone and older foundations, spring brings raccoon mothers, and fall brings the annual push of squirrels trying to establish winter attics. We remove humanely, seal with durable materials, and point out the tree limbs and vents that will cause the next problem if they are left as they are.
